drug_name: Netupitant and Palonosetron / Fosnetupitant and Palonosetron
what_its_for: This medicine helps prevent nausea and vomiting caused by cancer chemotherapy (chemo). It works by blocking signals in your body and brain that trigger the feeling of nausea and the urge to vomit. It is used both before and after your chemo treatments to keep you as comfortable as possible.
how_to_take: The oral capsule form (netupitant/palonosetron) should be swallowed whole with a full glass of water about 1 hour before your chemotherapy starts. You can take it with or without food. The intravenous (IV) form (fosnetupitant/palonosetron) is given to you by a nurse or doctor through a vein as an infusion over about 30 minutes, also about 30 minutes before your chemo begins. Do not crush, chew, or open the capsule if you are using the oral form.
dosing: Oral capsule (Akynzeo): One capsule (containing netupitant 300 mg and palonosetron 0.5 mg) taken by mouth once, about 1 hour before chemotherapy on Day 1 only. IV infusion (Akynzeo for injection): One vial (containing fosnetupitant 235 mg and palonosetron 0.25 mg) given through an IV over 30 minutes, starting about 30 minutes before chemotherapy on Day 1 only. Your doctor may also prescribe a steroid (such as dexamethasone) to be taken alongside this medicine to further control nausea. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: This medicine is usually given as a single dose before each chemotherapy session, so a traditional 'missed dose' situation is uncommon. However, if you forget to take the oral capsule before your chemo, contact your doctor or nurse right away. Do not take an extra dose on your own without being told to do so by your healthcare team. If your IV dose was missed or delayed at the clinic, your healthcare team will handle it for you.
storage: Oral capsules: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the capsules in their original blister packaging and away from moisture and heat. Keep out of reach of children and pets. IV form: This is stored and prepared by your healthcare team at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this at home. Dispose of any unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about local take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice or eating grapefruit while using this medicine, as it can increase the amount of drug in your body and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid alcohol, as it may worsen dizziness. Tell your doctor about ALL medications you are taking, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements, because this drug can interact with many other medications such as certain antidepressants, antibiotics, antifungals, blood thinners, and heart medications. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or drowsy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat; severe dizziness or fainting; muscle twitching, stiffness, or loss of coordination; confusion or agitation; hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there); high fever or sweating (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called serotonin syndrome); severe constipation or stomach pain; difficulty urinating; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if your nausea or vomiting is not controlled.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 1 hour of taking the oral capsule or within 30 minutes of receiving the IV infusion. It is designed to prevent nausea and vomiting both in the first 24 hours after chemo (called 'acute' nausea) and in the days that follow (called 'delayed' nausea, which can last up to 5 days after chemo). Most people notice good nausea control starting from the time of their chemo treatment and continuing for several days afterward.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before taking this medicine. Older adults (65 years and older): No dose adjustment is usually needed, but older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been well established; use is generally limited to adults. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustment is typically required for mild to moderate kidney or liver disease, but tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have, as severe liver impairment may require extra caution.
